samples.text:
The graph shows the world fish production from wild capture and from aquaculture between 1980 and 2020, and it is measured in million tonnes.

In 1980, wild capture was 68 million tonnes and aquaculture was only 5 million tonnes. So wild capture was much more bigger than fish farming at the start. Wild capture increased to 86 million tonnes in 1990 and it reached the highest point of 94 million tonnes in 2000. After that it was quite stable and it changed only a little, between 89 and 92 million tonnes. In 2020 it was 90 million tonnes.

On the other hand aquaculture grew all the time. It was 13 million tonnes in 1990 and 32 million tonnes in 2000. After 2000 it grow faster, it was 58 million tonnes in 2010 and 76 in 2015. In 2020 it reached 88 million tonnes which is almost same as wild capture.

Overall, wild capture was always higher than aquaculture, but aquaculture increased very much and at the end there was only a small difference between them.
samples.why: Relevant overview but placed at the end · key trends covered with some repetitive detail · adequate vocabulary with repetition of 'million tonnes' · double comparative, comma splice and article errors.

samples.text:
The line graph illustrates changes in global fish production from two sources, wild capture and aquaculture, over a forty-year period between 1980 and 2020.

Overall, wild capture remained the larger source throughout, but its output levelled off after 2000. By contrast, aquaculture grew continuously and rapidly, so that by 2020 the two methods were producing almost the same amount of fish.

In 1980, 68 million tonnes of fish were caught in the wild, compared with just 5 million tonnes produced by fish farms. Wild capture rose steadily over the following two decades, reaching a peak of 94 million tonnes in 2000. From that point on, it remained fairly stable, fluctuating between 89 and 92 million tonnes, and it stood at 90 million tonnes in 2020.

Aquaculture, on the other hand, showed uninterrupted growth. Production climbed to 32 million tonnes in 2000 and then accelerated considerably, reaching 58 million tonnes in 2010 and 76 million tonnes five years later. By 2020, fish farming produced 88 million tonnes, which means the gap between both methods had narrowed from 63 million tonnes in 1980 to only 2 million tonnes.
samples.why: Clear overview contrasting plateau and growth · key features well presented · logical progression · good use of derived comparisons · generally accurate language with an occasional awkward phrase.

samples.text:
The graph depicts the quantity of fish produced worldwide through wild capture and aquaculture, measured in million tonnes, from 1980 to 2020.

Overall, while wild capture accounted for the greater share of production throughout, it plateaued from around 2000 onwards. Aquaculture, by contrast, expanded relentlessly and by 2020 had almost drawn level with the traditional method.

In 1980, the wild catch totalled 68 million tonnes, dwarfing the mere 5 million tonnes supplied by fish farming. Over the next twenty years, wild capture grew steadily, peaking at 94 million tonnes in 2000. Thereafter, it stagnated, hovering within a narrow band of 89 to 92 million tonnes and finishing the period at 90 million tonnes.

Aquaculture followed a markedly different path. Its output rose modestly at first, to 13 million tonnes in 1990, before gathering pace and reaching 32 million tonnes in 2000. Growth accelerated further in the following two decades, with production jumping from 44 to 76 million tonnes between 2005 and 2015. By 2020, fish farms were generating 88 million tonnes, over seventeen times their 1980 level and only marginally below the volume of wild-caught fish.
samples.why: Key features skilfully selected and contrasted · clear, well-placed overview · accurate figures supported by apt derived comparisons · wide, precise vocabulary · varied, error-free structures throughout.
